tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in a message from the system. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.description:

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:

- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly.     name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }

  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

< **Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.

Both lie below `Numeral`, a sibling of the number types under `Number`. No numeral value exists when a program runs, so a numeral type has no getters, no `asFloat`, no `asString` and no `=` with a number type. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude follows the same design (P-37).

Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.
 
-**Under walk a numeral has a run-time class.** The checker types an integer numeral as `IntLiteral`, a sibling under `Number` that converts to the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` (P-76). Walk gives a numeral the class `Int`, `Long` or `BigNum` by its value. These classes stand for `ZZ32`, `ZZ64` and `ZZ`, but a generic instantiates at the class: `Box[\Int\]` is not `Box[\ZZ32\]` (row 364). Walk answers `IntLiteral`'s arithmetic as a `ZZ32` (row 578). The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or `Matrix` only at the eight number types, not at a user subtype of `Number`. Elsewhere they give a plain array, whose `+` and unary `-` fail dispatch under walk. Under walk, an inferred element type is a run-time class, so they give a plain array (row 721). Write the static argument.
+Elsewhere the numeral takes its default: `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where its value does not fit, and `RR64` with a radix point. Elsewhere includes an untyped binding, `Any`, `Object`, `Number`, `Index` and an unbounded type parameter. So `n = 3000000000` is a `ZZ64`, and `Cell(0.5)` is a `Cell[\RR64\]`. The default stays the value's type: for `x = 0.1`, `q: QQ = x` is refused. A type parameter that numerals alone fix takes the narrowest default that holds them all. A `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value, other than a numeral type's number, is a `ZZ32`, so `u: NN32 = n` is refused (P-173, P-40). Such a parameter of 2^31 or more is a `ZZ64` under walk, and raises an error on the compiled path (row 962).

Promotion instantiates a generic declaration at the narrowest type into which all its arguments coerce (P-74). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". Where the tied declarations differ only at the positions of the call's numerals, the checker reads the numeral as `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` where the value does not fit.

A program's own number type takes a numeral through a coercion generic over its numbers, which its body declares, as `value object Byte(b: ZZ32)` declares `coerce[\nat n, nat r, nat v\](x: NaturalNumeral[\n, r, v\]) where { v < 256 } = Byte(v.asZZ32)`. The coercion's body reads `n`, `r` and `v` as `ZZ` values without a bound, since a numeral's digits fit no fixed width (P-173, P-40). The `where` clause bounds the numerals that the type takes. A negative constant, as `-3`, reaches the type as the type's prefix `-` on the coercion's result for `3`, so a type without `-` refuses it. The coercion gives one value for each place where the numeral is written, and each run of that place reuses it (P-176). Without such a coercion, the type refuses a numeral. The library's factories `array1` and `array2` give a `Vector` or a `Matrix` only at the eight number types; at a program's own number type they give a plain array. `interpreter.md` and `compiler.md` give the other departures from these rules.

A folded comparison is a boolean. Any other result is one exact constant, which converts as a numeral does at one of the eight number types, or takes its default. So `2147483647 + 1` is the `ZZ64` 2147483648, not an `IntegerOverflow`, `(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3)` is `true`, and under walk `lr = 1/1000` is a `QQ`. So `h: Half = 10/20` needs `coerce(q: QQ)`; a numeral coercion is not enough. `||` of string literals folds into one literal (P-171). So `f[\T\](a: T, b: T)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` runs at `ZZ64`. Walk does not promote the elements of a tuple or varargs: it takes their join (rows 395, 511). Where several declarations apply only by coercion and none is more specific, both paths stop: "Ambiguous coercion". If one of them takes the call's numerals at their default, it runs instead: `1.0 s` for `s: ZZ32` is `RR64`'s product, not `QQ`'s.

So generic code over `T extends Number` can call on a `T` no method or operator that the number types declare, `asFloat` among them. Two numbers of different types compare by `=` only where a coercion carries one into the other: the library declares `=` for each such pair, so a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` of equal value are `=`. Otherwise `=` is `SEQV` ("Traits and objects"), and answers `false` without an error, as for a `ZZ64` against an equal `RR64`. A numeral reaches a number type's own `=` by its coercion (P-46). So on both paths `u = 0` and `0 = u` are `true` and `u =/= 0` is `false` for a zero `u: NN32`, and `h = 0.5` is `true` for `h: QQ = 1/2`. At a negative exponent, 1 and -1 give their power, 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and other bases raise `IntegerOverflow`. For a result that is not an integer, write `2.0^(-1)`, or a `QQ` base as `(2/3)^(-1)`, not `10^(-k)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has integer powers only at `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64`, each with an exponent of its own type; its `RR64` power takes an `RR64` or a `ZZ32` exponent, a negative one included. Its `ZZ32` power gives 0 at a negative exponent for other bases. At a base of 0 it throws a Java exception that no `catch` sees (rows 441, 523).

For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. Convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.
+**`/` on two integers answers a `QQ`.** So `7 / 2` is `7/2`, not 3. Truncate with `DIV`, on both paths. `DIV` answers its operands' type and rounds toward zero. For a float, make one operand a float, as `(1.0 s) / n` for `ZZ32` values `s` and `n`. No coercion carries a `ZZ64` into `RR64`, so convert each `ZZ64` operand with `asFloat`, as `asFloat(s) / asFloat(n)`. Until the switch-over, the compiler's library has no `QQ` and declares `/` only at `RR64`, so a compiled `7 / 2` is a static error.

 A clause form is a reduction or comprehension with generators in brackets, as `SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)`.
 
-**A reduction's static argument depends on the path.** The checker does not infer it for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, whose bound names the parameter (row 731). Write it in every clause form, as `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Other reductions take their bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types. If that join is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1". Departures under walk:
+**Where a reduction's bound names its parameter, as for `SUM`, `PROD`, `BIG MAX` and `BIG MIN`, the two paths fix an unwritten static argument from different places.** The argument is written as in `SUM[\ZZ32\][j <- 0#n] f(j)`. Without it, the checker takes the reduction's expected type, and the body's type only where there is no expected type or it does not fit the reduction's bound. So `x: RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#n] f(j)` sums `ZZ32` elements in `RR64`, not in the body's type. A reduction whose bound does not name its parameter takes its bound, or the expected type where the bound does not fit. Walk instantiates a reduction at its value's declared type: a local variable's, or a top-level or local function's return type, also where the clause form ends a block. A method's return type, a field, a top-level variable, a parameter and an assignment do not direct it. Else walk takes the join of the elements' run-time types; if it is outside the reduction's bound, each `+` runs at its operands' types. An element that does not convert to the instance stops in `__bigOperator`, "body param 1".
+
+At a method's return type, a field, a top-level variable and an assignment, the checker reads the declared type, so the two paths sum in different types (row 1008): `meth(): RR64 = SUM[j <- 0#4] huge(j)` raises `IntegerOverflow` under walk only. Write the argument there in a program for both paths. A call's argument has no expected type where the call is accepted without one. So as a call's argument, a reduction sums in its body's type on both paths. Write both arguments of `BIG MIN_MAX`, the element types of its pairs, as `BIG MIN_MAX[\ZZ32, ZZ32\][j <- 0#3] pr(j)`: the checker infers only a single static parameter (row 1007). Departures under walk:

-- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (rows 20, 717);
+- a comprehension inside another clause form is built at its elements' run-time types (row 717);
 - a written static argument that is not a number type ends an empty `SUM` in `CastError` (row 436).

Besides a `Boolean`, it takes a `Maybe` as an `if` condition, `Just` as true and `Nothing` as false. It refuses any other value. The specification and the checker take only a `Boolean`, so do not write a `Maybe` condition. The compiled path's own limits are in `compiler.md`.

Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays. The paths differ on `tint[\T extends Red\](x: Box[\T\])` beside `tint[\T extends Blue\](x: Box[\T\])`, where `Red`, `Blue` and `Box` are objects. The checker refuses it, because `Box[\Bottom\]` lies in both domains, and walk loads it. No decision says which is right. Assert neither path's answer in a test (ledger row 786).
128	- A `where` clause's constraint: the checker checks a function's or functional method's constraint on its own static parameters at the call. At a dotted call, a candidate is not applicable where the receiver's static argument breaks the method's constraint. A trait's or object's own constraint is checked where its type is used, also at a constructor call; only the checker reads it, and the compiled code does not check it. A `where`-clause variable is a static parameter of the function's arrow type, inferred at the call. The checker does not yet check these, and no ledger row holds the first two:
129	  - at a dotted call, a constraint whose bound names the method's own static parameters or a `where`-clause variable;
130	  - at a type's use, a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable;
131	  - a static argument written at a top-level call, against its parameter's bound (ledger row 470).
132	- A reduction without its static argument, whose bound names its parameter, such as `SUM`: the checker reports a type error in its body as the big operator's refusal, 'is not applicable to an argument of type ()' (ledger row 1015). Write the static argument to read the body's error.
133	- Imports: `import A.{...}`, with the three dots written, imports every name of `A`. The overloading check also reads `A`'s declarations of a name that the component imports by name from another api. So `import A.{...}` beside `import B.{ pick }`, where both apis declare `pick(x: P)`, is refused: 'There are multiple declarations of pick' (ledger row 813). Leave the name out of the whole import, as `import A.{...} except { pick }`.
134	- An `except` clause leaves out each identifier that it lists, on both paths. Neither path leaves out an infix operator that it lists. So where a component lists `-` in `except` and declares its own `-` at the api's parameter types, the code generator stops. Walk runs the component's own `-` (ledger row 814).
135	- Conditional extension: the condition holds while the checker checks the `extends` entry itself, an object's value parameters and every member. It does not hold for the other `extends` entries, the static parameters, the declaration's own `where` clause, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses. The checker lets a member that it checked under the condition be called where the condition fails (ledger row 773).
136	- A `comprises` clause that lists a type at a `where`-clause variable, as `NatParam comprises { N[\n\] } where [\ nat n \]` or `AnyList comprises List[\E\] where [\E\]`: at a call, the checker gives the variable a fresh size or type, equal only to itself. Two values passed in one call get two. A fresh type is bounded by the binding and by the clause's constraints. The variable is in scope in the trait, except in its `extends` and `excludes` clauses. The checker gives no fresh type where it meets the trait as a supertype of another type. Where a generic type that the clause lists, as `List[\E\]`, gives the body of a member of the trait, the code generator crashes: 'E is not in the kind env' (ledger row 812). Where the variable is a size, a compiled call that passes a value of such a trait where a listed type is expected fails the JVM's verification (ledger row 307). Departures: a fresh type also under a function type's result (ledger row 751), none for an extender that the clause does not list (ledger row 752), and a crash at a call, from outside the trait, of a member whose type names the variable (ledger row 756).
137	
138	## The `fortress` commands
139	
140	`Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.
141	
142	- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
143	- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
144	- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
145	- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.
146	
147	## Running
148	
149	    cd ProjectFortress
150	    # after an ant compileAll that started the caches again: the library order (build-and-caches.md)
151	    ../bin/fortress compile <path>/P.fss
152	    ../bin/fortress run P [args]
153	
154	A small program compiles in about 5 s and runs in about 1 s.
155	
156	- A crash of the checker prints one line and hides the Java stack. To see the stack, put `-debug stacktrace` before the file: `../bin/fortress compile -debug stacktrace <path>/P.fss`.
157	- A failed compile of a program leaves a 0-byte jar in `bytecode_cache/`. A run of the program then prints "Could not load P" and "Resource not found". Read the compile's error instead.
158	
159	## Before an edit
160	
161	Two notes under `explorations/coordinator/map/` help you find where a fix belongs. A status or a line number in them can be stale. Before you rely on a status, read the ledger rows that it cites. Before you rely on a line number, grep for the method's name.
162	
163	- Before you add or fix a language feature, print its row of the feature table. WORD names the feature, such as `spawn`, `coercion` or `typecase`. A row is about 1 KB. It names the feature's section of the specification, its parser rule, checker class, walk site, code-generator site, prelude declaration and ledger rows.
164	
165	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:spec-to-implementation.md#Feature by feature@WORD'
166	
167	- If your edit is in one phase, and you need what runs before and after it on each path, print that phase's section. Name the section by its number and the first word of its title. A section is 1 to 3 KB. B.1 is the phase list, B.4 disambiguation, B.5 desugaring, B.6 type checking, B.7 overloading, B.10 the caches, B.11 the runtime and B.12 the natives.
168	
169	      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'map:modules-and-phases.md#B.5 Desugaring'
170	
171	- Before you change the text of a diagnostic, grep the `.test` files for it. A `.test` file can pin a whole diagnostic with `compile_err_equals`, its `file:line:column` included. `grep -l 'TEXT' ProjectFortress/*tests/*.test`, with words of the diagnostic as TEXT, lists the files that pin it. Update each of those in the same commit. A line that you add to or remove from a compiler test program moves the pinned spans below it.
172	
173	## Testing an edit here
174	
175	- For a quick loop on an edit of the checker or the code generator, compile the edited class into a scratch directory, and run the compiler with that directory first on its class path. Give each run a fresh copy of the caches, because nothing checks the caches against the compiler that wrote them, and a compile of an unchanged program with a jar writes nothing:
176	
177	      Q=$PWD/tmp/quick ; export FORTRESS_CACHES=$Q/caches ; CP=$(bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
178	      mkdir -p $Q/classes && javac -nowarn -cp "$CP" -d $Q/classes ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/<path>/X.java
179	      rm -rf $Q/caches && cp -a default_repository/caches $Q/caches
180	      java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -Dfortress.caches=$Q/caches -cp "$Q/classes:$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell compile P.fss
181	      bin/fortress run P
182	
183	  For a Scala file, compile it with `java -cp "$CP" scala.tools.nsc.Main -classpath "$CP" -d $Q/classes -encoding UTF-8 X.scala`. Then put the edit into the tree and build it for real.
184	- If your change is near transactions, top-level mutable state or the class loader's first load, do the four-thread atomic runs (`gate.md`).
185	
186	## The checker's time
187	
188	This section is for a change of the checker: its Scala under `scala_src/`, or `ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast` and the generators under `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/`, from which the build generates the checker's syntax tree and `Walker`.
189	
190	The count stage takes `<out-file> <scratch>` and about 80 to 180 seconds, more under load. It can run past the Bash tool's 120-second limit, so run it in the background (`session.md`). It writes a table to the out-file: the errors of each api, the total, the number of places with errors, and the first crash. It keeps the checker's whole output in `<scratch>/run.txt`, and its caches in `<scratch>`, so a run from the base build leaves the base build as it was.
191	
192	The checker checks every api first, and the component only if no api has an error. In each api or component, it stops at the first of its stages that finds errors. The stages run in this order (`compiler/StaticChecker.java`, `checkCompilationUnit`):
193	
194	1. The type hierarchy and the type check.
195	2. The overloading check, which also compares the overloads' return types.
196	3. In the component only, the export check (`library.md`, "Designing a change").
197	
198	So the count misses the errors of the later stages, and a fix of an early error can raise it.
199	
200	The table's rows tell a clean run from a run that the checker did not finish:
201	
202	- `#total 0` and `#locations 0`: the checker reached the component and found no error.
203	- `#stopped`, in place of `#total` and `#locations`: the errors came from a phase before the checker, such as the parse. The checker reported none and did not reach the component. The script exits 1, and the gate reads the table as red.
204	- `#crash`: the first crash of the overloading check that the run survived, or `none`.
205	
206	If the run printed no error total and was not clean, the script writes no table and exits 1.
207	
208	The checker's results are the programs that it accepts and refuses, and each error with its text and its place. On the interpreter's library, a change keeps the results the same if both of these hold:
209	
210	- The two tables are equal: `diff` prints nothing.
211	- The two `run.txt` files are equal after you replace each run's own tree path with one word, such as `TREE`. Any difference fails.
212	
213	A node's hash starts from its class name, so an order in the output, such as the apis' checks, does not vary from run to run. A moved order is a difference: keep the old order, or report it.
214	
215	`Walker`, in the generated `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/FortressAst.scala`, is split into methods under 8,000 bytes of bytecode. HotSpot does not compile a longer method, and the walker runs on every node. `MethodSizeJUTest` fails if a method of the build grows past the limit, except the methods that its source lists in `listed(...)` entries. Run it alone with `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=MethodSizeJUTest`. If a method of `Walker` fails, lower `WALKER_CASES_PER_METHOD` in `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/ScalaAstGenerator.java`. If another method fails, split it under the limit. List it only if nothing in the checker or a compiled run calls it, with its size and what runs it, and name it in your report.
216	
217	The timing is a smoke test, to catch a slowdown of several times. One run of each tree is enough. A small difference, or one within the noise from run to run, is not a finding. In your report, say what you saw, and do not analyse it.
218	
219	If you change the checker:
220	
221	1. Make the change correct, with its tests. Commit it, and name the commit in your report.
222	2. Time the base build and the change, named `base` and `change`. Run the base in a call set up for the base build (`build-and-caches.md`), and the change in a call set up for your tree, each in the background (`session.md`). Use the same command for both, with `N` the run's name:
223	
224	       export W=<your tree> N=base ; mkdir -p $W/tmp/count
225	       time explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh $W/tmp/count/$N.txt $W/tmp/count/$N
226	
227	3. Make a second pass that makes the checker faster. Start with a profile (below). Where the profile shows a gain, take it. Where it shows none, say so in your report, with the profile's top frames.
228	4. If the second pass changed code, run the count stage once more with the command of step 2, named `pass`. Show that its results are the same as `change`'s. Then run `ant testQuick` once more (`tests-running.md`, "When to run a whole suite"). If it changed nothing, run neither, and report `change`'s results in place of `pass`'s.
229	5. If the pass reuses an answer that the checker computed earlier, as a memo does, audit it on one full run. Put the audit in an instrumented copy ("Testing an edit here"), never in the tree. In the audit, compute each reused answer again and compare the two. If any answer differs, the reuse is wrong: fix it or drop it, then repeat step 4. Report the count of reuses and of differences.
230	6. In your report, give each run's seconds, the diff of the `base` and `change` tables, the comparison of their `run.txt` files, and that `pass` has the same results as `change`.
231	
232	To find where the time goes, use JFR on the count stage's checker, instrumented copies compiled into a scratch folder ahead of the build on the class path, and the methods over 8,000 bytes that `MethodSizeJUTest` lists in its source. A profiled or instrumented run is neither a timed run nor a run to compare. Print the commands of two earlier speed probes (about 8 KB):
233	
234	    explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed-2/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings' 'doc:explorations/perf-probes/checker-speed/REPORT.md#Decisions, findings'
235	
236	If your brief asks you to review a change of the checker, run the count stage yourself. Time the base build and the worker's commit of step 1 once each, as step 2 says, with the commit and the worker's head in worktrees seeded at them (`worktrees.md`). Check that your times are the worker's, in order of size. Check that the commit's and the head's results are the same.
237

# The compiled checker, the code generator and the runtime

**count stage**
: Script that runs the compiled checker over the interpreter's library, on the `FortressLibrary` component and the apis that it imports, and prints the errors in a table: `explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/run.sh`. Its total is the checker count.

**distance stage**
: Stage of the gate that runs the compiled checker over fourteen components of the interpreter's library, `FortressLibrary` among them, runs each of the checker's steps on each component whatever the earlier steps report, and prints the errors in a table. Your brief gives its command when you need it.

The code of this area is in these directories:

- `scala_src/typechecker/`: the type checker, in Scala.
- `compiler/`: the disambiguator, the desugarers, overloading, `codegen/`, `NamingCzar` and `OverloadSet`.
- `runtimeSystem/`: `InstantiatingClassloader`, tasks and transactions.

The phases' names in the code are parse, PREDISAMBIGUATEDESUGAR, DISAMBIGUATE, GRAMMAR, PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR, INTEGERLITERALFOLDING, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR, OVERLOADREWRITE and CODEGEN.

## What the two paths share

After the phases, each path has its own code for these:

- Values: walk's `interpreter/evaluator/values/` (`FInt`, `FFloat`), and the compiled `compiler/runtimeValues/` (`FZZ32`, `FRR64`).
- Number natives: walk's glue classes, in `interpreter/glue/prim/` (`Int.java`, `Long.java`).
- Dispatch: walk searches at run time, in `OverloadedFunction`. The compiled path calls a dispatch method that `OverloadSet` generates.
- The run: `fortress run` starts a second JVM (`bin/run`), which never enters `Shell.java`.

Both paths run the helpers, the public static methods of classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

The phases differ too: walk turns off some desugarings that the compiled path runs (`interpreter.md`, "Where a fix of walk belongs"). A fix of one of those desugarers changes only the compiled path.

## The compiler's prelude, until the switch-over

The compiled path uses the compiler's own prelude: `LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss`, `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` and `Library/CompilerAlgebra.fss`. `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`.

Do not add a declaration to the three prelude files: the switch-over deletes them, and their tests stay. Two exceptions (P-37): its numeral types and coercions follow `revival-changes.md`, "Numbers", and a brief may ask to declare each built-in number type as one `value object`, the form that both libraries are to take. If a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the one library binds is wrong, fix the helper's Java, even if the prelude binds it, and leave the prelude's text: its binding gives the fix. Change with it a compiled test that pinned the old result.

## What the compiled path cannot compile yet

For a construct that it cannot compile yet, the code generator calls `sayWhat` or throws another `CompilerError`. Such a call or throw is a code-generator wall. The code generator has no case for these constructs:

- `label` and `exit`, `spawn`, and `atomic` used as an expression;
- an object expression;
- an array literal, such as `[1 2 3]`.

It compiles a local function as a closure, also one that calls itself or another local function of its block. It refuses these forms (ledger row 304):

- a local function with static parameters of its own: 'Can't compile a local function with static parameters of its own yet';
- two local functions of one name in a block: 'Can't compile overloaded local functions yet';
- a local function with the `atomic` modifier: 'Can't compile a local function with this modifier yet'.

A type assumption `e asif T` has the value of `e`, but the call around it chooses its declaration as if `e` were a `T`, a supertype of `e`'s type (`Specification/basic/expressions/type-annotation.tex`). The code generator compiles one at a dotted call's receiver, at a call of a functional method or an overloaded function whose every argument is an assumption, and elsewhere as the value of `e`. It refuses these forms (ledger row 818):

- a call of a functional method or an overloaded function with an assumption at some of its arguments but not all: 'Can't compile a dispatched call whose arguments are not all type assumptions';
- a generic method on an assumed receiver: 'Can't compile a type assumption at the receiver of a generic method yet';
- a call of an overloaded generic function with an assumption at an argument: 'Can't compile a type assumption at a call of an overloaded generic function yet'.

It also refuses a function or method with a contract (`requires`, `ensures`, `invariant`). It compiles a declaration whose own header or `extends` entry has a `where` clause, and emits nothing for the clause. A call of a function or method whose own clause introduces a `where`-clause variable, as `where [\nat n\]` does, links, but dies at run time with `NoClassDefFoundError` (ledger row 867). `compiler_tests/XXXWhereVariableCallCompiled.test` records it: copy its form for such a call. The disambiguator, which both paths run, drops a trait's or object's contract, so the code generator never sees one, and walk does not check one either (ledger row 781). It refuses a function or method with a modifier other than `getter`, `setter`, `io`, `private`, `abstract` and `test`, such as `override` (ledger row 650). A trait or object that extends a generic trait compiles with `Any` as the static argument. With `Bottom`, `Self` or an abbreviated type there, the code generator refuses the declaration. An abbreviated type is a short form, such as `RR64[3]` for an array type. With a tuple that holds `Any` there, the code generator crashes (ledger row 889).

The compiler's prelude has no array types, only `ZZ32Vector` and `StringVector`. Its `for` loops, comprehensions and reductions work over `ZZ32` ranges only. Its reductions give a `ZZ32` or a `String`.

Until the switch-over, a compiled test uses none of these. If a test needs one, write it as an `XXX` test that names the wall (`tests-writing.md`).

## What the code generator does

- It emits no primitive `double` arithmetic.
- It runs a program's own `coerce` from a numeral once for each place where the numeral is written, in the component class's static initializer, except where the place's type names a type parameter (below). The runtime initializes the class of each component that the program's classes name before `run()`, in one task. So a coercion's output comes before the program's first line, and the parallel parts of a coercion's body run one after another there. A coercion that raises stops the program before `run()`. A test of a coercion that raises sets `run_exits_nonzero=true` (`tests-writing.md`).
- The class loader rewrites a template's bytes with ASM. The emitted classfiles stay at version 1.6, because this rewriting keeps no stack-map frames. Do not raise the version.
- The `value` modifier adds the mark interface `ValueObjectMark` to the object's class. The compiled `SEQV` (`nativeHelpers/equality.java`) reads the mark. The modifier does not inline or unbox the fields.
- An array of `RR64` values is to be stored as an unboxed `double[]`. The code generator does not build it yet. If your task touches how arrays are stored, print the two POSITIONS entries on arrays first (about 2 KB):

      explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'positions:array is stored as' 'positions:array design'

## The runtime

- The class loader is `runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java`. The revival has changed it for sizes and for the lock on a class's first load (ledger row 417). Before you investigate a failure while a class loads, read ledger rows 408 and 559, which name it (`records.md`, "Reading the record").
- The compiled code keeps each mutable variable in a cell (`compiler/runtimeValues/MutableFValue.java`). Before each read and write of the cell, the generated code asks `BaseTask.inATransaction()` (`runtimeSystem/`). Inside an `atomic` block, the access goes through the transaction. So the transaction tracks the variables that the block touches. From the switch-over, it also tracks each element of the one library's arrays, by array and index: `compiler/runtimeValues/FortressArrayStore.java` calls the transaction's methods `TXReadSlot` and `TXWriteSlot`. Walk does not run this class, so test an edit of it with `ArrayStoreJUTest`, beside it.

## Natives

`import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{...}` in a `.fss` file binds static Java methods over plain Java values.

A body `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.Class.method")` binds one such method, a helper, too. In a compile, at the parse, the compiled path, and not walk, rewrites the body as a call of the method through a generated `import java`, with `self` first in a trait or object (`compiler/BuiltinPrimitiveRewriter.java`). The checker then checks the declaration against the method's Java signature. In a compile, it reads `int` as `ZZ32`, `long` as `ZZ64`, `float` as `RR32`, `double` as `RR64`, `boolean` as `Boolean`, `String` as `JavaString`, `BigInteger` as `ZZ` and `Object` as `Any` (`NamingCzar.fortressTypeForForeignJavaType`). The compile stops in these cases:

- If the string is in that package but names no public static method: 'builtinPrimitive names no static helper: …'.
- If the string names a glue class or anything else outside that package: 'Variable builtinPrimitive is not defined.'
- If the declaration has a varargs parameter: the same message (ledger row 849).
- If the declaration is a local function or a method of an object expression: the same message. The rewrite reaches only a component's declarations and the members of its traits and objects (ledger row 865).

The rewrite runs only in a JVM that has made a Fortress repository of the compiled path, the compiler's store of components, not this git repository. Walk's repository switches it off again. `fortress compile` makes one, and so do `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` and `typecheck` (`Shell.compilerPhases`). `fortress parse` and `fortress api` make none, so they rewrite a body only after a compile in the same JVM (ledger row 882). Alone, they pass a misspelt helper. Test a binding with `compile`. In a suite, the result of `parse` or `api` depends on whether a compile ran earlier in the same JVM.

To test a helper on the compiled path, write a compiled test whose own declarations bind it, as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperBindingCompiled.fss` does. Until the switch-over, a compiled test cannot reach the interpreter's library's bindings.

The count stage and the distance stage check the interpreter's library with the same rewrite. There, the checker differs from a compile in these ways:

- A string that names a glue class, or a declaration with a varargs parameter, does not stop the check. The body stays a call of `builtinPrimitive`, typed at the declared result type, and no Java signature checks it (ledger row 849).
- The checker reads a helper's Java types as the interpreter's library's types: `String` as `String`, not `JavaString`, and the rest as in a compile.
- A component that imports a DSL grammar is parsed by other code (`GraphRepository.syntaxExpand`), which does not rewrite its bindings. So, as for a glue class, no Java signature checks them.
- The count stage checks only the `FortressLibrary` component's bindings. A binding of another component, as `FortressBuiltin`'s, only the distance stage checks.

The checker, in a compile and in both stages, reads `int` as `NN32` or `Char`, and `long` as `NN64`, only for six transfer helpers with fixed names (`NamingCzar.java:373-384`, `:494-503`). Where a binding gives a parameter, `self` or the result the type `NN32`, `NN64` or `Char`, or a parameter or `self` the type `UnsignedLong` (the one library's object that extends `NN64`), and the helper has `int` or `long` there, the rewrite passes that value through the matching transfer helper. A result declared `UnsignedLong` gets none. `self` gets a transfer helper only in a method of one of these four types itself. The transfer helpers return their argument unchanged. So the checker accepts such a binding whatever helper it names, a signed one included, as `simpleIntArith.intLT` for `NN32`'s `<`. If you move a binding over these types onto a helper, test it on both paths at values where a signed and an unsigned reading differ (2^31 and above for `NN32`, 2^63 and above for `NN64`), as `compiler_tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Compiled.fss` and `tests/NativeHelperFamilyNN32Walk.fss` do. If the class has more than one method of the helper's name and number of parameters, the rewrite adds no transfer helper. The checker then reports 'Could not check call to function builtinPrimitive_<Class>_<method>', followed by '… is not applicable to an argument of type …'.

The wrapper generator wraps every method of a class that it is given, the private methods too. If a type has no Fortress counterpart, it fails the whole import. So give every method of a helper class a signature that maps to Fortress, also a private method. In the count stage and the distance stage, a type maps only if the interpreter's library declares it. So there, a binding stops its component if any method of its helper's class has a type that only the compiler's prelude declares. The distance stage then counts the component as a stopped target. `nativeHelpers/systemOps` is such a class: its `getArgs` answers `StringVector`, so the message is 'FortressBuiltin.StringVector is undefined.' (F-321). Bind a helper of another class.

## Traps of the compiled path

- The compiler's prelude declares `print`, `println` and `String`'s `||` at `Object`, not `Any` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:37`, `:55`, `:61`). So until the switch-over, the checker refuses a generic that prints a value of a type parameter written without a bound, or concatenates it onto a `String`. The message names `Object`, as 'Object->() is not applicable to an argument of type T.' does for `println`. In such a generic of a compiled program or test, write `T extends Object`. The generic then takes no tuple, function or `()`. The one library declares these operations at `Any` or `String`, so do not change its text for this limit. The prelude's `||` takes the string first only, so `c || s` for a `Character` value `c` is refused (ledger row 965). Put a string first, as `("" || c) || s`.
- A `try`'s `forbid` clause lists exception types: an exception of a listed type that no `catch` clause took is wrapped in a `ForbiddenException`, which the `try` throws. A `try`'s `finally` clause does not run when an exception leaves the `try` block: one that no `catch` clause takes, or that `ForbiddenException` (ledger row 890). So write no compiled program that relies on `finally` after an exception leaves the `try`. A test that needs it is an `XXX` test (`tests-writing.md`). `Shell.java` dispatches `bin/fortress <command>`.

- To see what an early phase makes of a program, stop after that phase: `parse` (a syntax check), `disambiguate`, `grammar`, `desugar` or `typecheck`.
- `unparse` prints the syntax tree back as Fortress source. Use it to see what a desugaring made.
- `link` links a compiled component (the `link` step of a compiled `.test` file). `api` writes a component's api. `test` runs a program's `test` declarations under walk.
- The command chooses the library. Walk and `test` call `Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`. Every other command calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. Each call points `WellKnownNames` and `Types` to its prelude, and sets the desugaring switches.

    ../bin/fortress run P [args]

90	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
91	
92	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
93	
94	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.
95	
96	### The caches
97	
98	A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.
99	
100	- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
101	- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss" ...`.
102	- `analyzed_cache/`: the results of the phases that `fortress compile` reuses.
103	- `bytecode_cache/`: one jar for each compiled component.
104	
105	In the first three caches, `<hash>` is a hash of the source's absolute path, and the entry holds that path. So the entries of a tree copied to another path must be renamed and rewritten. `explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh` does this (`references/worktrees.md`).
106	
107	`references/build-and-caches.md` says when a run reuses an entry, and when the build empties the caches.
108	
109	### Parallelism and mutable state
110	
111	Fortress evaluates in parallel by default, not in Java's left-to-right order. The iterations of a `for` loop, the elements of a tuple, and the arguments and operands of a call can run at once. A loop is sequential only if every generator is `seq(...)`. The parallel parts run as tasks on a work-stealing pool, the fork/join pool of Doug Lea (a `java.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool`). `FORTRESS_THREADS` sets its number of threads. Tasks, transactions and the pool are built twice, independently: for walk in `interpreter/evaluator/tasks/`, and for the compiled path in `runtimeSystem/`.
112	
113	`x = e` declares an immutable variable. `var x: T = e` and `x: T := e` declare a mutable one, and `x := e` assigns to it (`Specification/basic/variables.tex`). These are Scala's `val` and `var`, or Swift's `let` and `var`. A field is immutable unless it is declared with `var`. A value object is a tuple, `()`, or an object whose declaration, or a trait that it extends, has the `value` modifier, as the library's numbers, characters and booleans do. It has only immutable fields and value semantics, like a Swift `struct`. Any other object, except a function, is a reference object, like an instance of a Swift class. Each construction makes a new reference object, distinct from all others (`Specification/basic/objects.tex:24-33`).
114	
115	Parallel code stays free of races in these ways:
116	
117	- Most data is immutable.
118	- A big operator, such as `SUM` or `BIG MAX`, combines the results of its tasks, as OpenMP's reduction clause does. No task writes a shared accumulator. The specification's reduction variables are not built.
119	- A write to shared state goes inside an `atomic` block. This is software transactional memory, like Haskell's `atomically` (`Specification/basic/evaluation/parallelism.tex`). The programmer writes `atomic`; the compiler adds none.
120	- Tasks can write different elements of one array in parallel (`Specification/basic/memory-model.tex`, "Programming Discipline").
121	
122	So `acc := acc + x` inside a parallel `for`, with no `atomic`, is a race. The suites run at four threads, once each, so a race can show in them. A passing run does not prove that there is none.
123	
124	Inside an `atomic` block, the compiled code tracks each mutable variable that the block reads or writes. From the switch-over, it also tracks each array element that the block reads or writes (`references/compiler.md`).
125	
126	## Fortress as a language
127	
128	Each point below corrects an assumption from a language that you know. `references/tests-writing.md` gives the form of a program.
129	
130	- **Dispatch is on every argument, at run time.** A call chooses among overloads by the run-time types of all its arguments, as in Julia, not by static types as in Java. The checker accepts two overloads only if their parameter types exclude each other, one is strictly more specific, or a third covers their meet. The more specific one's return type must fit the other's. Walk checks part of this at load.
131	- **Functional methods.** A method with `self` among its parameters is called `f(x)`, not `x.f()`. It overloads with top-level functions. Most operators are declared so: `opr +(self, other: T): T`. A functional method's name is reserved in every program that imports it, so do not name a variable after it. One type must not have a dotted and a functional method of the same name.
132	- **Traits and objects, no classes.** A trait has methods and abstract fields, and extends several traits. An object is a leaf. `excludes {A, B}` says that no value has both types. `comprises {A, B}` says that every value has a listed type, near Scala's `sealed`. No type may extend two instantiations of one generic trait. This exclusion rule is why the number types are flat (below).
133	- **Static parameters.** They are written `[\T\]`, and `[i]` indexes. Their kinds are types, sizes (a `nat` or `int` parameter used as a value is a `ZZ32`, but a `ZZ` where it is one of a numeral type's numbers: `references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"), `bool` and `opr`. Generics are invariant: there is no `+T` or `-T`. An unbounded type parameter is bounded by `Any`, which holds tuples, functions and `()`, as `Object` does not. A type parameter that a call does not fix takes its bound. Under walk, one whose bound names the parameter itself stays open, and every value passes it. Walk instantiates a reduction or a comprehension without static arguments at the type declared for its value: a local variable's type, or a top-level or local function's return type. Without one, it uses the join, the least common supertype, of its elements' run-time types. Some other cases still get the empty type `Bottom` under walk (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Static parameters").
134	- **Numbers are siblings, not a tower.** `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN32`, `NN64`, `ZZ`, `QQ`, `RR32` and `RR64` are siblings under `Number`. None is a subtype of another, unlike Haskell's classes or Java's widening. A wider type declares a `coerce` from each narrower one. A conversion does not change which declaration runs when one already fits. A numeral is the one exception: it can run a more specific declaration that its coercion reaches. Overflow raises `IntegerOverflow`, but an expression of numerals alone folds exactly (`references/revival-changes.md`, "Numbers"). The algebra is self-typed traits, such as `AdditiveGroup[\T\]` with `+`, not monoids over an operator parameter. `references/library.md` gives the rest: ranges, wrapping, `SUM`.

9	## Dispatch and overloading

11	**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.
12	
13	**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.
14	
15	**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".
16	
17	**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780).

19	**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:
20	
21	- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
22	- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.
23	
24	The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method is an overload for this rule too. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. ## Dispatch and overloading

**Overloads may differ in their static parameters (P-45).** An example is `ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T` beside `ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T`. The Working Draft forbids such pairs. A declaration's declared domain is the set of argument types that its declared parameter types accept at some instance within its bounds: every `Shape` for the first `ident`. The checker applies the overloading rules of `SKILL.md` to declared domains. The more specific declaration's return type must be a subtype of the other's at every instance that the argument types allow, not at one only.

**Where a declaration has static parameters, exclusion is read over the whole tuple of parameter types (P-152).** By the exclusion rule, a value has at most one instance of a given generic type. So where both declarations name the same generic type at a position, a value of both domains makes the two static arguments equal. The domains exclude where these equalities cannot hold together, or where some position excludes at the instance that they force. So `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, with `P[\T\] excludes { Q[\T\] }`, is valid. Both paths refuse a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free, as `o[\T, U\](x: Q[\U\], b: Box[\T\])` beside the first `o`: nothing ties `U` to `T`. In its test of whether two domains exclude each other, the checker puts the meet of a static parameter's declared bounds in the parameter's place where the parameter is a whole parameter type, an element of a tuple or a member of an intersection or union (P-157). Inside a static argument, as `T` in `Box[\T\]`, the parameter stays.

**Walk chooses by declared parameter types, never by the order of the declarations.** It compares declared domains where one lies strictly inside the other. Otherwise it compares the instances that the call makes. It infers a dotted generic method's static arguments from the arguments' run-time types, as for a generic function. A trait's generic method called with an argument outside a bound fails with "Cannot unify".

**Walk's load check is not the verdict of these rules.** It refuses some valid pairs and loads some invalid ones, and the checker differs from it on others. Before you change code to pass walk's check, or take its acceptance as proof, find the case in `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks": a case that cites a ledger row is a departure of walk. For example, walk compares two functional methods of a generic trait or object at each call, not at load (row 780).

**Two functional methods with equivalent parameter types are duplicates, wherever `self` stands.** So the checker refuses `f(self, y: S)` beside `f(x: S, self)` in a trait `S`. Abstract declarations count:

- both paths refuse an abstract and a concrete method with the same parameter types in one trait;
- both paths refuse an object that inherits an abstract functional method from one trait and its body from another, unless the object declares the method itself (P-149). The Scala language accepts it.

The Meet Rule asks for a declaration that covers the meet of two overloads that neither exclude each other nor nest (`SKILL.md`, "Fortress as a language"). An abstract functional method is an overload for this rule too. So the checker refuses `h(self): ZZ32` in a trait `S` beside a top-level `h(x: String): ZZ32`: nothing covers the meet of `S` and `String`. Likewise, a program's trait that declares its own functional `+` overlaps the library's `+` between an array and a number, because a type can extend both the trait and `Number`, which has no `comprises` clause (P-160). Declare the trait `excludes { Number }`, or make it exclude arrays, `excludes { HasRank }`. Or declare the `+` in an object, not in a trait: an object excludes every trait that it does not extend, because no other type can extend it. Otherwise walk refuses the program at load: "fails the Meet Rule". The checker refuses such a pair in one component, but accepts it against the library's `+` (row 918). Give a trait with its own functional `-`, `MIN` or `MAX` the same fix: the library declares these in the same form.

## Traits and objects

**The compiled checker applies the exclusion rule (P-43, P-97).** It refuses a type that extends two instantiations of one generic trait. Walk does not apply the rule: it runs such a type, and refuses overloads on two instantiations, as `g(b: Tg[\3\])` beside `g(b: Tg[\4\])`, because it does not read them as excluding (row 416). The specification marks the Working Draft's examples that break the rule "Not allowed": do not copy them.

**A `comprises` clause speaks of values (P-60).** Every value of the trait that declares it is a value of a listed type. So a generic trait need not be listed if every type below it is below a listed type, as `Integral[\I\]` below `AnyIntegral`. A Java `permits` list names each direct subtype; this clause need not. So where the Meet Rule asks for a declaration at the meet of two overloads, several declarations that together cover the meet serve. At load, walk checks extenders only against the clauses of the program's main component (row 551).

**`override` widens.** An `override` overrides an inherited declaration only where the inherited parameter types are strictly narrower than its own. To replace an inherited declaration at its own parameter types, declare it again without `override`. An `override` in a trait also overrides in every type below it. The checker checks that an overriding return type is a subtype. Walk refuses at load an `override` that, by this rule, overrides nothing, so a Java-style `override` in the library stops every program. Two departures: the checker accepts such an `override` (row 653), and the code generator refuses every `override` modifier, so a program that writes one does not compile (row 650).

**An object defines an inherited abstract method by bodies that together cover its parameter types (P-147).** It needs one body at those types, or several narrower bodies that cover them, with `comprises` clauses read. Walk refuses at load an object without static parameters that leaves one uncovered. Walk skips this check for a generic object (row 665). Walk and the checker stop the search for a cover at the limits that `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", gives. The checker refuses a cover by several bodies where the abstract or a covering method has static parameters (row 725).

**In a self-typed trait the checker types `self` as the trait met with the implementing type.** A trait `T` is self-typed if both conditions hold:

- `T` has no `comprises` clause, or one that lists only `...`;
- `T` has a parameter `X` bounded by `T` itself, as `trait T[\X extends T[\X\]\]` (P-146), or by a self-typed trait `U[\X\]` that `T` extends, as `trait T[\X extends U[\X\]\] extends U[\X\]`.

In `T`'s bodies, `self` has the intersection type of `T[\X\]` and `X`. So `floor(self): I = self` in `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]` is valid without a cast. The checker refuses a type that extends `T[\A\]` and is not an `A`. A compiled body of `T` that returns `self` at `X` runs, also where `X` is an object type. Three shapes still fail when the class loads:

- a function expression or a local function that returns `self` at `X` fails the JVM's verification (row 1050);
- a conditional with `self` in one arm and another value in the other fails the JVM's verification (row 1051). `StandardTotalOrder`'s `MIN` and `MAX` have this shape (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:291-292`). The integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` declare their own;
- a default body that calls a method on a value of type `X` gives a `ClassCircularityError` where the object lists `T` first in its `extends` clause (row 1052).

For the first two shapes, bind `self` to a variable of type `X` first, as `s: X = self`, and use `s`. This workaround has run only in a trait with a `comprises` clause, as `r: R = self` in `trait Q comprises { R }`, so run it before you keep it. For the third shape, declare the method in `T` without a body, and give the body in the object. Declaring it again in the object while `T` keeps its body still fails.

## How a defect is recorded

Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:

1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.

I brought the `fortress-repo` skill in line with climb batch 31's landing in two commits. Lint passed with no hits on every changed file. Nothing is pushed.

## Commits

- `33ecda80af`: the orientation update, installed in `revival-changes.md`, with its lines in `sources.md`.
- `16472318bf`: the other parts (`SKILL.md`, `compiler.md`, `interpreter.md`, `gate.md`), with their lines in `sources.md`.

## Sections installed from the orientation

The judge said "install" for the whole text, so no section is held. Two sections changed. `revival-changes.md` went from 31,052 to 32,054 bytes, which matches the judge's figure.

- **"Traits and objects".**
  - **Wrong before:** it said that a compiled body of a self-typed trait that returns `self` fails the JVM's verification. That stopped being true when row 695 was fixed.
  - **Now:** such a body runs. Three shapes still fail when the class loads (rows 1050, 1051 and 1052), and the section gives a workaround for each.
  - **The judge's correction:** I put in the sentence that the judge wrote for row 1052. The writer's text said "declare the method in the object". A run shows that this form still fails while the trait keeps its body. The text now says: "For the third shape, declare the method in `T` without a body, and give the body in the object. Declaring it again in the object while `T` keeps its body still fails."
- **"Dispatch and overloading".** The P-152 rule is worded more narrowly. It now refuses "a pair whose exclusion needs a static parameter that the equalities leave free". This is wording only.

## Sentences changed

**`compiler.md`** (34,241 to 37,041 bytes):

- **"What the compiled path cannot compile yet":** the list said that `label`, `exit` and `atomic` as an expression do not compile. They compile now. Only `spawn` is left on the list (F-373, F-374). I checked `CodeGen.java`: `forLabel`, `forExit` and `forAtomicExpr` exist, and there is no `forSpawn`.
- **"The runtime":** this now says that an object's `var` field is also kept in a cell, which the object holds (F-374, row 641).
- **"Traps of the compiled path":**
  - A `finally` clause is also skipped when an `exit` leaves the `try` (row 890).
  - A `label` block or an atomic expression as a later argument of a call also fails verification (row 322).
  - New sub-bullets under the numeral traps:
    - a `label` block whose value joins a numeral with a `ZZ32` (row 340);
    - an atomic expression whose value is a numeral (row 1043).
  - New bullets:
    - an `exit` out of an `atomic` block, and an `exit` after its `label` block has completed (rows 1039, 1041);
    - a functional method with `self` not first (rows 573, 1038);
    - a `value` object with a `var` field (row 112).
  - In the `NoSuchMethodError` list, "Two calls die" became "These die". A third case was added: an assignment to a `var` field of a value whose type is strictly below the field's type (row 1053).
- **"The checker's gaps":** three new bullets:
  - the Return Type Rule at a tuple of object types (row 1048, F-75);
  - a tie between generic candidates, whose result changes with the order of the suite (rows 499, 1046, 1047);
  - a generic self-typed trait's method reached along two paths (row 1037, F-372).

**`interpreter.md`** (24,081 to 24,897 bytes):

- **"How walk evaluates a program":** an object's field of arrow type and a declared arrow return type also keep a generic value (row 1036).
- **"What walk checks":** three new departures of walk's load check (F-375):
  - a plain declaration that writes no return type is not judged (row 1044);
  - no `comprises` clause is read (row 550);
  - a pair over an arrow type loads (row 1049).

**`gate.md`:** the atomic runs now list twenty-four programs, not twenty-two. `AtomicExprCompiled` and `AtomicFieldCompiled` are added, as in the gate's summary and the batch script's list.

**`SKILL.md`:**

- **"Parallelism and mutable state":** a transaction now tracks an object's `var` field too (F-374).
- **"The caches":** the quoted cache entry now says "It starts `(Component @"`, then the source's absolute path." The old quote named a real file, `Library/FlatString.fss`, and the harness attached that whole file to every agent that loaded the skill.

## Choices I made

- **Rows 1048 and 1037.** The data asked for these in `revival-changes.md`. But the task also said to change nothing else in that file, and the file is far over its size budget. So I put them in `compiler.md`, "The checker's gaps", where the compiled checker's other gaps are. The other ways:
  - add them to `revival-changes.md` and break the rule of the install;
  - leave them for the next orientation round.
- **F-375 in `revival-changes.md`.** No sentence there is false. The section already points to `interpreter.md`, "What walk checks", which now holds the new departures. So I left it as installed.
- **The tie between generic candidates (rows 499, 1046, 1047).** I wrote the fact only. I added no rule such as "keep such a call out of a gated test", because that would change the meaning of `tests-writing.md`, which is yours to judge.
- **Row 1041.** I wrote that the rules do not settle the question. I added no "assert neither path's answer", because a plain test of the compiled answer exists (`ExitAfterLabelCompletedCompiled`).

## Already true, and lines I could not place

- No line of the data was already true.
- I placed every line, except the one on `tests-writing.md`, which I left for you.

## For the coordinator

- **`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded", the second way:** I did not change it. The question is how to record a defect that no gated test holds in every order of the suite. That is a change of a rule's meaning, and the data asks you to judge it first.
- **Row 1040:** under walk, a `catch` of `Exception` takes an `exit`. The record lists it, but the data does not name it, so the skill has no sentence for it.
- **Other skills:** I found no sentence in another skill that the landing made false.
- **The orientation round:** the judgement's carried points stay open. Among them are the `SEQV` sentence (2.2) and the size of `revival-changes.md`, which is about 2.7 times its budget.

99:A place fixes a type when its declared type has a coercion from the numeral type, as each of the eight number types has. Such places are a typed binding, an assignment, a field, a parameter and a declared return type. At a number type, the numeral converts from its exact value: exactly into the five integer types and `QQ`, and with one rounding into `RR64` and `RR32` (P-76, P-172). So `u: NN32 = 5` binds, and `q: QQ = 0.1` is `1/10`. A numeral outside the type's range, or that rounds to an infinity there, is refused: by the checker statically, by walk when the place runs. Walk's message depends on the place: a top-level binding gives 'Type mismatch binding', a parameter 'got arg'. To get an infinity, overflow run-time arithmetic: for `t: RR64 = 10.0^308`, `t TIMES 10.0` is `Infinity` under walk. `x.isInfinite` tests for one. Until the switch-over, the compiler's prelude declares neither `TIMES` nor `isInfinite`.

content.text:
I fixed 26 of the cold reader's 30 flags in one commit, `e64da5d944`, and left 4. Lint passed with no hits on every changed file. Nothing is pushed.

## What a worker would have done wrong, and what the text says now

**`SKILL.md`**
- **"The caches":** the start of a cache entry gave the source's path, which the next paragraph already says. It now gives only `(Component @"`.
- **"Parallelism and mutable state":**
  - A worker on walk does not load `compiler.md`, so it would not learn that an `exit` out of an `atomic` block loses the block's writes. This holds on both paths, so the sentence and its workaround (set a flag, exit after the block) moved here.
  - The same reader could think that something refuses a `var` field in a value object. The text now says that nothing refuses it, so give it none.
- **"Fortress as a language":** the Return Type Rule is now named where the rule is stated. A worker on the compiled path met the name in `compiler.md` with no definition.

**`compiler.md`**
- **"The runtime":** "also an object's `var` field" could be read as a second cell beside the variable's. It now says that the field is kept "in a cell that the object holds".
- **"Traps of the compiled path":**
  - **The `finally` clause:** "or that `ForbiddenException`" had no verb. The text now lists the three things that skip the clause: an `exit`, an exception that no `catch` clause takes, and the `ForbiddenException` that the `try` throws.
  - **"Atomic expression":** the term was used before any example. It is now defined where it first appears: `atomic e`, as `atomic 1`.
  - **A `label` block that ends in a numeral:** the old text did not show `exit ... with`. It also did not say to end the block with the typed variable, so a worker could bind the numeral and still fail. It now says both. I checked this against `XXXLabelNumeralValueCompiled.fss`.
  - **An atomic expression with a numeral value:** "a place of declared type" is now "a place that fixes a type", the term of `revival-changes.md`. The text now also says that the checker refuses it.
  - **`LabelExit` and `LabelException`:** neither name was explained. `LabelExit` is now named as the Java exception, which no `catch` clause takes. `LabelException` is named as the library's, which walk's `catch` takes.
  - **The self-not-first overloads:** the old text did not say which code tests what. It now says that the compiled dispatch method tests the receiver's type where it should test the other argument's. It then gives each of the two results with its row.
  - **The `var` field assignment:** the example's `T` read as a type parameter. The example now declares `trait T`.
- **"The checker's gaps":**
  - **The tuple-domain pair:** "a pair" after "a tuple" could mean the tuple. It is restated as "a pair of declarations".
  - **The tie:** "the head of its sort" named no sort. It now says that the checker sorts the candidates and keeps the first. It also says what to do: if a compiled test passes alone and fails in the suite, look for such a tie first.
  - **The method reached along two paths:** the chapter that does not settle it is now named by its file, `Specification/basic/traits.tex`. The bullet now ends "Assert neither path's answer in a test", as the part says for row 786.

**`gate.md`, "The atomic runs":** the count of programs is cut, because the loop's list gives them and the count must change each time the list does.

**`interpreter.md`, "What walk checks":**
- "Plain declaration" and "object type" were unclear. The first item now says "without static parameters", and that `NN32` is an object type in walk's library. I checked this in `FortressBuiltin.fsi:132`.
- The second item now says that `ZZ64` is the trait that comprises the one object `Long`.
- The third item now says why the arrow pair breaks the Return Type Rule. A function of type `Any -> Circle` is also a `Circle -> Circle`, and at that instance the generic one returns `Any -> Circle`. This is from row 1049.

**`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects":**
- The rule "declare it again without `override`" now warns that the checker refuses this where an object reaches a generic self-typed trait's method along two paths (row 1037).
- "Also where `X` is an object type" and "still" are cut. They told what the fix changed, not what to do.
- **`MIN` and `MAX`:** a worker could not tell when they fail, or what its own type should do. The text now says that they have this shape from the switch-over, because the compiler's prelude declares neither (`CompilerAlgebra.fss:17-23`). It says that a compiled type that extends `StandardTotalOrder` declares its own, as the integer types, `QQ` and `RR64` do.
- "Default body" is now defined: a body that `T` gives one of its methods.
- The sentence on where the `s: X = self` workaround has run is cut. Its example was not a self-typed trait, and its only action was a test run, which a worker does anyway.

`revival-changes.md` is now 32,123 bytes.

## Flags left

- **`compiler.md`, the exit after its `label` block has completed: "assert neither path's answer".** A plain test, `ExitAfterLabelCompletedCompiled`, already asserts the compiled answer, so this would contradict a test that the gate runs. The alternatives:
  - add "assert neither" and change that test;
  - add "assert only the compiled answer".
- **`compiler.md`, the tuple-domain pair: "a compiled test of it is an `XXX` test".** `tests-writing.md` already gives that rule, and no workaround is on record.
- **`interpreter.md`, whether a `var` field keeps the generic value.** Row 1036 measures only an immutable field. The record does not settle the `var` case.
- **`revival-changes.md`, "Dispatch and overloading", the P-152 rewording.** The judge checked the installed wording against P-152. The proposed wording could change the rule's meaning.

## Decisions not taken

- **The tie between generic candidates:** I added only the diagnostic ("look for such a tie first"). I did not add the proposed action, "make one candidate more specific". No record shows that it works.
- **The two-path refusal:** I added "assert neither path's answer". It follows the part's practice for undecided cases. The record says only that the case is not decided.
- **The workaround sentence:** I cut the sentence on where `s: X = self` has run. The judgement said it could go once the regression key's run at the self-type parameter is on record. That run is in `key.md`, which is modified but not committed in the working tree. The alternative was to keep the sentence until the key is committed.

## For the coordinator

- The regression key (`key.md`) is still uncommitted. The cut workaround sentence rests on its run.
- The `MIN` and `MAX` instruction rests on P-47 and on the judge's check of the compiler's prelude. No run of a compiled type that declares its own `MIN` and `MAX` is cited.
